transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Mendes (Redwood AE), Leah Park (Redwood SE), Dr. Aisha Karim (HelixArc Head of IT), Marc Dufour (Cloud Architect), Sandeep Rao (Security Ops)

Summary (auto): HelixArc wants a non-cloud-mixed footprint for EU research data; needs clarity on how Redwood enforces region pinning and what happens during capacity or network incidents when fallback to US might occur. Also asked about KMS key locality and audit trails for CIP/PHI investigations.

[00:00] Carlos Mendes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Carlos from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Dr. Aisha Karim: Aisha here, thanks.
[00:10] Marc Dufour: Marc, hi.
[00:12] Sandeep Rao: Sandeep on my side.
[00:15] Leah Park: Leah from the SE team — I'll cover technical bits.
[00:18] Carlos Mendes: Great. Our goal today is to run through region pinning options, KMS approaches, and the subprocessor list. We'll try to capture concrete next steps.

[00:30] Marc Dufour: So problem statement: HelixArc runs EU-hosted research workloads involving de-identified but sensitive assay outputs. Legal requires EU-residency for at-rest and in-flight processing whenever possible; however we need to understand the behavior if an EU region is out of capacity.
[00:46] Carlos Mendes: Yep, that’s common. There are a few configurations — strict geofence, region affinity with soft fallback, and hard-blocked routing. Leah, could you describe how those look in practice?
[00:56] Leah Park: Sure. So strict geofence means requests are only accepted in the designated region; Redwood will reject requests that would route out — we return an explicit 409/region-restriction. Region affinity prefers EU nodes but will failover to US nodes if you enable cross-border fallback, which is useful for availability but has compliance implications. We can also do a hybrid: for certain routes you can block cross-border processing (for example model inferences that touch regulated fields), and allow non-sensitive routes to fallback.
[01:25] Dr. Aisha Karim: Is there a way to audit when fallback happens? We need that for our incident response and for regulators.
[01:33] Leah Park: Yes. All routing decisions are logged — timestamp, source region, chosen endpoint, and the policy that triggered it. Those are emitted to the audit stream and also available in the Console per-route. You can export logs to your SIEM (we support CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Elastic/Kafka).
[01:48] Sandeep Rao: Are those logs residency-bound? I mean if a fallback hit the US, do the logs themselves cross borders?
[01:56] Leah Park: Good question. The primary logs for routing and decision metadata can be replicated to your EU logging endpoint only — we can configure log sinks so the primary copy remains in region. However certain platform-level telemetry (health pings) may be aggregated in our control plane — we offer an option for a private control plane in Private deployments to keep telemetry in your VPC. For hosted, we can provide filters so sensitive fields are not exported out.
[02:23] Marc Dufour: Okay. For KMS — we need keys to reside in EU, ideally in our HSM. Can we BYOK and enforce that model weights or caches are encrypted with our EU-only keys?
[02:35] Leah Park: Yes. We support customer-supplied keys via KMS integrations — both cloud KMS and customer-controlled HSM through vault integrations. You can scope keys per-tenant and specify that certain artifacts (eg model checkpoints, persistent KV cache) are encrypted with the EU KMS. Runtime ephemeral caches still use short-lived keys, but you can set a policy that prevents any key material from leaving the region.
[02:58] Carlos Mendes: Note — runtime KV cache sometimes gets mis-reported in docs; we make sure ephemeral cache isn't persisted. If you want absolute guarantee, Redwood Private lets you host both serving and control plane inside your VPC so keys never transit Redwood's network.
[03:12] Dr. Aisha Karim: If we use hosted but with BYOK, what's the trust model? Who holds the root key?
[03:18] Leah Park: Typically HelixArc would hold the root in its KMS/HSM; Redwood is given per-session encrypt/decrypt tokens via standard KMS APIs. We also support split-key where part of key material is held in your HSM and part is derived transiently in the runtime — reduces blast radius. We can provide the architecture doc.
[03:35] Sandeep Rao: What about cross-border backups and snapshots? We must prove backups are EU-resident.
[03:42] Carlos Mendes: We can configure storage class to be EU-only for snapshots and backups. If a customer needs no cross-border backups, we set snapshot retention in-region and restrict export. For enterprise contracts we have eu-only data residency clauses.
[03:55] Marc Dufour: And subprocessors — litigation found an issue where a sub-processor in the US handled logs. We need an up-to-date list and contract commitments.
[04:06] Leah Park: Right. We'll send the CSV with sub-processor names, their function, and country. For each subprocessor we can indicate whether they process metadata or content. For anything that crosses borders we can show the legal basis and DPA addendum.
[04:19] Dr. Aisha Karim: Will you require a contract addendum for any subprocessor change?
[04:23] Carlos Mendes: We provide notification windows per our enterprise contract; we can add a clause for HelixArc to require prior written approval for changes affecting EU residency. That can go into the SOW.
[04:33] [05:00] (background noise)
[05:10] Marc Dufour: If we pin requests to eu-west-1 and that region loses capacity, what's the exact behavior? Do you queue, reject, or failover automatically?
[05:20] Leah Park: Depends on policy. Modes: 1) Reject — immediate 409 with an explanatory body; 2) Queue and retry — we can enqueue for a small window (typically seconds) until capacity recovers; 3) Soft failover — route to next best region (us-east) but mark the request as exported and log for audit. We recommend soft failover only if you accept cross-border processing; otherwise reject or queue.
[05:44] Sandeep Rao: For queued requests, what about data residence of the queued copy?
[05:48] Leah Park: Queues are region-scoped if you select strict residency. Queue replicas won't be created cross-border unless you enable geo-replication for availability. We'll show you the queue config options in the runbook.
[05:58] Dr. Aisha Karim: SOC2 — can you expose evidence that region pinning is enforced?
[06:03] Carlos Mendes: Our SOC2 evidence includes change logs on routing policies, audit trails for configuration changes, and deployment manifests. For Private deployments we can include runbooks and access logs. For hosted, we provide redacted artifacts and auditor-friendly extracts.
[06:20] Marc Dufour: On RBAC and SSO — our security team wants SAML + SCIM and RBAC per team plus LAUD (least admin rights). How fine grained is Redwood's RBAC?
[06:30] Leah Park: You can map SAML groups to roles and set route-level permissions. We support role inheritance and granular policy: read-only monitoring, deployment engineer, crypto admin (KMS ops), etc. SCIM provisioning works with major IdPs.
[06:42] Sandeep Rao: Logging retention — regulators ask for 7 years in some workflows; what's max retention and cost?
[06:49] Carlos Mendes: Console supports retention policies up to multi-year on opt-in, but long-term retention is typically delivered via export to customer's long-term store (S3 in eu-west) — we can help automate lifecycle rules. For long retention we usually bill for storage and ingestion.
[07:05] Marc Dufour: For the perf test — we'd like to simulate EU traffic and force a US fallback to measure PII handling and latency. Is there tooling?
[07:13] Leah Park: Yes, we'll provide a small harness: a synthetic load generator configured with headers to pin locations, and an option to toggle fallback policy. We'll also capture traces and annotated audit logs.
[07:26] Dr. Aisha Karim: Anything else about encryption in transit?
[07:29] Leah Park: TLS 1.2+ by default, mTLS for service-to-service, and per-route client certs for private deployments. You can also enforce TLS termination within your VPC if you go Private.
[07:40] [08:00] (overlap)
[08:10] Sandeep Rao: How do you handle subpoena/NDAs — if US jurisdiction demands data, can Redwood assert region locks?
[08:19] Carlos Mendes: Legal matters are complex. For hosted we respond per our DPA and law enforcement request process; for strict EU-only physical control the Private deployment gives you the strongest position — we can ensure data and keys are under your control, minimizing Redwood access. We can walk through the legal flow with your counsel.
[08:37] Marc Dufour: On split-key — is that supported with AWS CloudHSM and on-prem HSM simultaneously?
[08:43] Leah Park: We have patterns and some references — split-key can be orchestrated via Vault + plugin to CloudHSM or on-prem HSM. We'll include a reference architecture.
[08:53] Dr. Aisha Karim: Ok let's be pragmatic. We prefer hosted initially but can't tolerate unapproved cross-border processing for sensitive routes.
[08:59] Carlos Mendes: Totally reasonable. We'll recommend a hybrid config: hosted with route-level blocking for regulated endpoints, BYOK with EU KMS for stored artifacts, and a Private control plane to keep routing decisions and telemetry in EU.
[09:14] Marc Dufour: Can you provide a binding statement about no-data-exfil unless explicit fallback is enabled by us?
[09:20] Carlos Mendes: We can provide contractual language in the DPA that disallows automatic cross-border processing for specified routes and requires customer opt-in for any fallback.
[09:29] Leah Park: Also, we'll show how to configure alerts so if any request is about to fallback the on-call is paged and the request can be rejected automatically.
[09:38] Sandeep Rao: Great. What about pricing impacts — EU-only pools and Private control plane — is there a delta?
[09:45] Carlos Mendes: Yes, there is typically an incremental cost for reserved EU-only capacity and Private control plane hosting. We'll include a cost delta in the proposal.
[09:53] Marc Dufour: Final question: what's the lead time for Private control plane setup?
[09:58] Leah Park: Typically 6–8 weeks from contract signature, depending on network setup and KMS onboarding. We can do an accelerated path but it requires more upfront infra work.
[10:12] Carlos Mendes: Ok let's recap next steps — (1) Redwood to send region pinning runbook + subprocessor CSV; (2) Redwood SE to produce perf test harness; (3) HelixArc to circulate policy and lists. We'll sync early next week.
[10:27] Dr. Aisha Karim: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:30] Meeting end.
